I would be of the opinion that any means is valid to express emotion. Music, which derives from maths, is a language. We started by smashing rocks and sticks together. One time is a sound, two times is a beat, and three starts a rhythm. It evolves from there and is guided by the emotions of the player. So yes, electronic music is "real" (whatever that means). Even when someone doesn't care for a particular piece, or even has an unpleasant response, it is still transferring an emotion and that is a language.

As for "cheating", I presume you may mean that some prefer and appreciate the talent to play an instrument or vocals deriving from trained practice and dedication. I certainly do. The "message" of said derivement speaks more to me, more depth of communication. But in the end, if an emotion is transferred, the means and import is up to the listener to assign. Hardly an easy subject to discuss.

Lol not an easy topic at all.

Now that the question is out there, I don't think electronic music is cheating at all. One still has to understand basic music theory; rhythm, dynamics, pitch, etc to be able to manipulate those machines. It's not just as simple as pushing a button as many in my circle believe it to be.

Mastering a certain instrument is a commendable feat in itself, but one still only has that instrument's timbre and specific quality to contend with. With electronic sound modules, an artist can go well beyond the normal scope of sound generated by a certain instrument.

Re your last paragraph: It's been called "chasing sound". I can be moved by the basic sounds of a particular instrument, and am appreciative of an artist that can explore all facets that instrument can produce. I don't think it invalidates an expression to seek even further modifications to extend the "voices" that instrument can create. At some point even that is exceeded and new ways to generate sounds are devised.

Let's take it to one extreme. We are now at the point that AI is "creating music". Is the programmer of the AI considered an artist, even though they may have no direct expression of the output? I contend that the reception, not necessarily the production, is most valuable. If you derive enjoyment from sounds, isn't that the criteria that matters?
